title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
1.1 Problem Statement

1.1.1 The Problem:
Autonomous-vehicle pick-up / drop-off (PUDO) maneuvers — the moments a driverless vehicle stops so a rider can get in or out — are a plausible source of curb-space conflict, minor collisions, and rider complaints. Whether that risk is growing, shrinking, or holding steady as a fleet scales is hard to answer from the public record: California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) AV Deployment reports are large, redacted, and change format from quarter to quarter, so nobody has simply lined them up into a rate over time.


1.1.2 Contribution

A reproducible pipeline (pudo-pipeline) that ingests nine CPUC quarterly report zips for Waymo’s driverless deployment — two incompatible file schemas, redaction, and formatting drift included — into five analysis-ready tables.
An exposure-adjusted PUDO complaint rate across eight quarters (2024 Q3 – 2026 Q2), on trips — the team’s chosen exposure measure, cross-checked against total vehicle miles traveled — with an explicit primary trend test (Negative-Binomial GLM, after Poisson regression was diagnosed as overdispersed), a launch-period sensitivity analysis isolating the 2024 deployment ramp, a distribution-free cross-check (Mann-Kendall), and a Bayesian refit (PyMC/NUTS) that reports a direct posterior probability the rate is declining alongside the frequentist p-value.
A placement of the PUDO hazard on a probability × impact risk matrix that is computed from the data rather than asserted, with the probability basis left as a visible, toggleable assumption.



1.1.3 Scope and Vision
Scope: one carrier (Waymo), one state (California), eight quarters, public CPUC filings only — no proprietary telemetry. Vision: the pipeline’s loaders are written against the CPUC’s public template, not against Waymo specifically, so the same numerator/denominator/trend method can be pointed at any other CPUC-reporting AV carrier to support carrier-to-carrier comparison rather than a single-carrier trend.

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
1.2 Technical Challenges

Two incompatible numerator schemas. 2024 reports ship one aggregate, pre-summed row per quarter; 2025Q1 onward ship ride-level microdata (millions of rows) with a Y/N complaint flag. Both had to be reconciled into one numerator, and the level shift between eras cannot be fully ruled out.
Redaction. Incident timestamps, locations, and the PUDOTravelLane flag are blank in every file of every period, ruling out within-quarter timing or spatial analysis.
Silent formatting drift. Comma-grouped numerics, filenames that change across quarters, and a transposed carrier ID silently nulled the exposure data until caught — the loader now warns loudly instead of nulling quietly.
Non-calendar reporting periods. The 2024 CPUC reports are not calendar quarters, so “2024 Q3” / “2024 Q4” needed explicit relabeling (period_label, is_calendar_quarter) to avoid silently comparing the wrong months.
Small, overdispersed counts. 27–79 complaints per quarter is enough to rule out the normal-approximation trend test, but not enough to ignore quarter-to-quarter noise.

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
3.1 Data Sources
Public data comes from the CPUC AV Program’s quarterly deployment reports (cpuc.ca.gov → Licensing → Autonomous Vehicle Programs → Quarterly Reporting) [1]. Two file families, both filed per reporting period:

Incidents-Complaints — the numerator. PUDO complaint and PUDO-collision counts.
Month-Level — the denominator. Real Year/Month, trips, and vehicle miles traveled (VMT). VMT is further split into three “period” columns in the source file, but CPUC’s own reference key never defines what those periods mean, so this analysis uses trips as the primary exposure measure and VMT only as an unsplit, whole-quarter cross-check.

Nine raw reporting windows (Jun–Aug 2024, Sep–Nov 2024, a Dec 2024 one-month stub, then eight calendar quarters through 2026 Q2) are recombined into eight analysis quarters, 2024Q3–2026Q2.
The pipeline’s two upstream file families reduce to a single hand-off table, final_pudo_summary — one row per analysis quarter, carrying only the complaint numerator and the trips denominator (Table 1). This is the dataset the rest of the paper’s analysis runs on:

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
4.1 Feature Engineering
Every analysis period carries a clean sort/filter key (period_id) alongside a human-readable label, its exact date window, and a flag for whether that window is actually a calendar quarter (period_label, window_start/window_end, is_calendar_quarter — false only for the two 2024 periods). Two exposure denominators are computed per period — trips (one pick-up + one drop-off per trip, the most literal PUDO-opportunity count; the primary measure) and total VMT (a cross-check) — each paired with a pudo_per_100k_* rate, plus a PUDO-share-of-all-complaints column for context.

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
4.2 Modeling
PUDO complaints were initially modeled using Poisson regression with the logarithm of trip exposure included as an offset. A variance-to-mean dispersion diagnostic (Equation 3) showed substantial overdispersion in the quarterly counts (\(\text{VMR} \approx 5.9\)), violating the Poisson equidispersion assumption. Temporal trends were therefore estimated using Negative-Binomial regression with a log link and a trip-exposure offset as the primary model. Because only eight quarterly observations were available, the same model was additionally estimated in a Bayesian framework to more fully characterize parameter and dispersion uncertainty. The Poisson fit below is retained only as an initial diagnostic baseline — it is never reported as the trend result.

4.2.1 Poisson regression (initial diagnostic baseline)
The complaint count \(Y_t\) in analysis quarter \(t = 0, \dots, 7\) is first modeled as a Poisson process whose rate scales with exposure \(E_t\) (trips, or VMT as a cross-check), with a log-linear time trend:
\[
Y_t \mid \mu_t \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_t), \qquad
\log \mu_t = \log E_t + \beta_0 + \beta_1 t
\tag{1}\]
\(\log E_t\) enters with a fixed coefficient of 1 (an offset), so \(\beta_1\) is the log change in the underlying rate \(\mu_t / E_t\) per quarter, not in the raw count. Every incidence rate ratio (IRR) and “per-quarter % change” quoted in this paper, for whichever model produced \(\beta_1\), is:
\[
\text{IRR} = e^{\beta_1}, \qquad
\text{\% change per quarter} = \big(e^{\beta_1} - 1\big) \times 100\%
\tag{2}\]


4.2.2 Overdispersion check
Equation 1’s defining assumption is \(\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t]\). This is checked with the index of dispersion (variance-to-mean ratio, VMR) on the raw complaint counts across the \(n = 8\) quarters:
\[
\text{VMR} = \frac{s^2}{\bar{y}}, \qquad
D = (n-1)\,\text{VMR} \;\sim\; \chi^2_{n-1} \ \text{ under } H_0 : \text{Poisson}
\tag{3}\]
\(\text{VMR} \approx 1\) is consistent with a pure Poisson process; \(\text{VMR}
\gg 1\) — the result found here (VMR ≈ 5.9) — rejects equidispersion, so the Poisson fit’s confidence interval and \(p\)-value understate uncertainty and are not used for inference about the trend.


4.2.3 Negative-Binomial regression (primary trend model)
Because Equation 3 rejects equidispersion, the trend is instead estimated with Negative-Binomial regression (the NB2 parametrization used by statsmodels [2]), keeping the same log-linear mean structure and offset as Equation 1:
\[
Y_t \mid \mu_t, \alpha \sim \text{NB}(\mu_t, \alpha), \qquad
\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mu_t + \alpha\,\mu_t^2, \qquad
\log \mu_t = \log E_t + \beta_0 + \beta_1 t
\tag{4}\]
with the dispersion parameter \(\alpha\) estimated by maximum likelihood alongside \(\beta_0, \beta_1\) (larger \(\alpha\) means more overdispersion relative to Poisson under this parametrization). This is the paper’s primary frequentist trend model, reported with \(\beta_1\), its standard error, 95% confidence interval, \(p\)-value, and the incidence rate ratio and percent change of Equation 2.


4.2.4 Launch-period sensitivity
2024 Q3–Q4 read as a deployment/launch ramp, with substantially higher exposure-adjusted rates than 2025 onward (Figure 2). Rather than simply discarding those quarters, Equation 4 is re-estimated — same model form, same trip-exposure offset — on two pre-registered windows to test whether they drive the full-period result:

A. Full period — 2024 Q3 – 2026 Q2 (\(n = 8\); the primary model above)
B. Post-ramp — 2025 Q1 – 2026 Q2 (\(n = 6\); excludes both 2024 quarters)

Comparing \(\beta_1\), its confidence interval, and its \(p\)-value across the two windows indicates whether the apparent decline is concentrated in the launch period or continues afterward. Given \(n = 8\), a simple two-window comparison is used rather than a piecewise or launch-indicator model, to avoid introducing more parameters than the data can support.


4.2.5 Exact (Garwood) Poisson confidence interval
Uncertainty around each observed quarter’s count is reported with the exact Poisson interval rather than the normal/Wald approximation, so it stays valid at small or zero counts:
\[
\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(k) = \left[\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^2_{\alpha/2}(2k),\;\;
\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}(2k+2)\right] \Big/ E \;\times\; 10^5
\tag{5}\]
where \(\chi^2_{p}(\nu)\) is the \(p\)-quantile of a chi-square distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom, \(k\) the observed complaint count, and \(E\) the exposure (trips) for that quarter. This interval is descriptive: it summarizes uncertainty around one observed quarter’s count/rate. It is distinct from — and not a substitute for — Equation 4’s inferential uncertainty about the trend across quarters; overlapping exact Poisson intervals between quarters do not, by themselves, establish that no trend exists.


4.2.6 Distribution-free trend check (robustness)
As a robustness check that assumes no particular count distribution — not a replacement for the primary Negative-Binomial fit — the Mann-Kendall trend test [3], [4] computes Kendall’s \(\tau\) between the quarter index and the per-quarter rate \(r_1, \dots, r_n\) (chronological order):
\[
\tau = \frac{2}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i < j} \text{sign}\big(r_j - r_i\big)
\tag{6}\]
\(\tau < 0\) agrees with a declining trend; its \(p\)-value is reported alongside, separately from the NB model’s.


4.2.7 Bayesian Negative-Binomial refit
Because only eight quarterly observations are available, Equation 4 is additionally estimated in a Bayesian framework to more fully characterize parameter and dispersion uncertainty — the frequentist fit instead estimates \(\alpha\) by maximum likelihood and then treats it as known, relying on a large-sample approximation that a sample this small may not support. The same likelihood and exposure structure as Equation 4 is refit as a full posterior (PyMC [5], NUTS sampler) with weakly informative priors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\beta_0 &\sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(\log(\bar{r}),\, 2^2\big) \\
\beta_1 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1^2) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\mu_t &= E_t \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 t) \\
Y_t \mid \mu_t, \alpha &\sim \text{NB}(\mu_t, \alpha), \qquad
\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mu_t + \mu_t^2/\alpha
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}\]
where \(\bar{r}\) is the pooled baseline rate and \(\beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) deliberately expresses no prior belief about direction. Note Equation 7’s variance term is the inverse sense of Equation 4’s \(\alpha\) (larger \(\alpha\) here means closer to Poisson) — the two are not numerically comparable. The model is sampled with 4 chains × 2000 draws, checked for convergence (\(\hat{R}\), effective sample size, divergence count) and for sensitivity to the prior width on \(\beta_1\). The quantity of interest is the posterior probability the rate is actually declining, estimated directly from the fraction of posterior draws below zero rather than from a \(p\)-value:
\[
P(\text{declining}) = P(\beta_1 < 0 \mid y_{1:n})
\tag{8}\]
This Bayesian refit is reported as a robustness / small-sample analysis alongside the frequentist estimate, not as a claim that it fits the data better: no model-comparison criterion (e.g. WAIC/LOO) or posterior-predictive check is computed here, so no such claim is made.


4.2.8 Risk-matrix probability basis
To place the PUDO hazard on a probability × impact risk matrix, three ways of expressing “how likely is a PUDO event” are compared, holding the impact reading fixed. Let \(k = \sum_t y_t\) be total complaints and \(N = \sum_t E_t\) total trips over the window.
Per-period — the probability of at least one complaint in a reporting quarter, treating the mean quarterly count \(\bar\lambda = k/n\) as a Poisson rate:
\[
p_{\text{per-period}} = 1 - e^{-\bar\lambda}
\tag{9}\]
Per-trip — the raw empirical per-trip probability:
\[
p_{\text{per-trip}} = \frac{k}{N}
\tag{10}\]
Bayesian — a Beta-Binomial posterior on the per-trip rate (Jeffreys-style \(\text{Beta}(0.5, 0.5)\) prior), converted to a predictive probability of at least one complaint in a future quarter of size \(E_{\text{next}}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{rate} \mid k, N &\sim \text{Beta}(0.5 + k,\ 0.5 + N - k) \\
p_{\text{bayesian}} &= 1 - e^{-\widehat{\text{rate}}\; \cdot\; E_{\text{next}}}
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}\]
using the posterior mean \(\widehat{\text{rate}}\) and the most recent quarter’s trip volume as \(E_{\text{next}}\).

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
6.1 Key Concepts and Definitions

PUDO — pick-up / drop-off: the maneuver where a vehicle stops to let a rider board or alight.
Exposure denominator — the activity measure a complaint count is divided by (trips or VMT) so rates are comparable across quarters of very different fleet size.
Overdispersion — when a count’s variance exceeds its mean beyond what a Poisson process allows, indicating real between-period rate variation.
Risk matrix axes — Probability: how likely the hazard is to occur in a given period; Impact: how severe the outcome is when it does.
Credible interval vs. confidence interval — the Bayesian model’s 95% credible interval is a direct probability statement (“there is a 95% chance the true slope is in this range, given the data and the prior”); the frequentist confidence interval is not, which is why the two are reported side by side rather than treated as interchangeable.
Descriptive vs. inferential interval — the exact Poisson interval on each observed quarter (Equation 5) describes uncertainty around that quarter’s count; the Negative-Binomial regression’s confidence interval on \(\beta_1\) describes uncertainty about the trend across quarters. They answer different questions, so overlapping per-quarter intervals are not evidence that no trend exists.

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
6.2 Assumptions

PUDO complaints are initially treated as a Poisson-type count process; the overdispersion test shows this assumption fails, so Negative-Binomial regression — not Poisson — is used for all trend inference.
The Bayesian trend model’s priors are weakly informative and were checked for sensitivity (Table 8) — the posterior does not depend meaningfully on the specific prior width chosen.
The risk matrix’s “Almost certain” probability reading assumes the relevant question is will at least one PUDO complaint occur somewhere in the fleet this quarter (it will), not the odds for any single trip.
Complaint counts are assumed complete and consistently defined within each reporting era; the 2024 aggregate table and the 2025+ ride-level microdata are assumed to measure the same underlying thing.

title: CurbRisk-AV — Quantifying autonomous vehicle pickup and drop-off risk using exposure-adjusted complaint data
text:
6.3 Limitations

Complaints are self-reported by the carrier to its regulator; the rate measures reported problems, not necessarily underlying PUDO behavior, and reporting propensity could itself change over time.
Waymo expanded to new cities during the window; a rate change may partly reflect new-market composition rather than a change in PUDO behavior.
The 2024 and 2025+ numerators come from different source-file schemas, so a level shift at that boundary cannot be fully distinguished from a real trend.
The launch-period sensitivity check further shrinks an already-small sample (post-ramp \(n = 6\)), which limits its power: a non-significant post-ramp slope is also consistent with a real but smaller decline continuing, not only with no decline at all.
Redaction removes all within-quarter timing and location detail, and the travel-lane PUDO signal is unavailable in every file.
Single carrier, single state, eight quarters — not yet a cross-carrier or multi-state comparison.
